front: What does the clip do for $A>0$?
back: Flat for $\rho>1+\varepsilon$: no incentive to raise a good action's probability further; still active if $\rho<1-\varepsilon$.

front: What does the clip do for $A<0$?
back: Flat for $\rho<1-\varepsilon$: no incentive to cut a bad action further; still active if $\rho>1+\varepsilon$.
The surrogate is a good approximation only near the old policy; large steps can destroy performance and the next batch is generated by the damaged policy.
Collect rollouts, compute and freeze advantages and $\log\pi_{\text{old}}$, do $K$ epochs of minibatch steps on the clipped loss, discard data, repeat.
$\lambda=0$: TD residual (low variance, biased). $\lambda=1$: Monte Carlo advantage (unbiased, high variance). 0.95 is common.
At episode end the bootstrap and the trace are cut: $\delta_t=r_t-V_t$ and $\hat A_t=\delta_t$.
SFT on demonstrations; reward model from preference pairs; PPO against the reward model with a KL penalty to the reference policy.
$P(y^+\succ y^-)=\sigma(R(y^+)-R(y^-))$; loss $-\log\sigma$ of the margin. Only reward differences matter.
The policy finds outputs the reward model over-scores but humans would not; the KL leash and fresh preference data counter it.

front: DPO and GRPO in one line each
back: DPO: closed-form preference loss, no reward model or PPO loop. GRPO: PPO-style update with a group-relative baseline instead of a critic, often with verifiable rewards.
